answer.rationale: With the line at 94% of committed volume and no buffer, any delivery interruption is costly, and switching primary vendors within a 14-day window carries unverified onboarding/ramp risk despite memory_c2's favorable account—that memory describes a different cycle and doesn't speak to performance under near-zero slack. Memory_c1 and c6 indicate the incumbent relationship is stable and has already yielded volume-based cost reductions without narrowing service scope, and memory_c4 shows that benchmarking against market quotes (here, the low-cost vendor's quote) is an effective lever to extract price and term concessions from the incumbent without migration risk. I verified c2 and c4 because they are the two memories most load-bearing for choosing between switching and negotiating: c2 to check whether the low-cost vendor's onboarding claim generalizes to a tight-capacity scenario, and c4 to confirm the mechanics of successful renegotiation are replicable now. Given the mandate is 18% and the low-cost quote alone meets it, using that quote as negotiating leverage with the incumbent may capture most of the savings while preserving delivery continuity, deferring the harder switch-vendor decision to when there is more schedule buffer to absorb transition risk. This is not a full rollout decision since it's a single contract renegotiation, but it is the primary lever available this cycle, so I don't treat it as a small guarded test either.
